title: 🛠️ Skunkworks at Atlas Corp
subtitle: Build a new product inside a Fortune-500 — without getting killed by the immune system
theme: Intrapreneurship: turn an internal idea into a funded business unit
description: You're a Senior Director at Atlas Corp ($14B revenue, 38,000 employees). You convinced the CEO to seed a $2M skunkworks to build a new B2B SaaS product the parent co could never ship — and now you have to actually deliver. Manage three sponsors at different VP levels, navigate the corporate immune system, raise stage-gated budget, and survive the steering committee. Six rounds. One product launch, or one termination notice.
learning_objectives: Run the intrapreneur playbook: sponsor mapping, stage gates, political capital
Defend ROI to a steering committee against internal alternatives
Build a coalition across functions when you have no formal authority
Recognize when 'corporate antibodies' (legal, security, finance) are blockers vs gates
Choose between killing your project on your terms vs being killed on theirs

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Each round is a quarter inside Atlas Corp. Read your sponsor map and political-capital meter.
Pick the option that progresses your stage-gate without burning sponsors or political capital.
Author your OKRs and SWOT when prompted — these are graded by a senior operator (LLM).
Pass the steering committee at the Q4 stage gate, or your funding runs dry.
tips: You can spend political capital but never get more. Choose battles.
Sponsor alignment compounds: a happy sponsor introduces you to their peers.
Don't fight legal — pre-empt them by inviting them in early.

target_audience: Corporate innovation leaders, MBA, accelerator participants

soundscape.description: R15 — corporate office hum + steering-committee cues for the Skunkworks sim.

psychological_framework.description: Intrapreneurship dimensions: political acumen, coalition building, stage-gate discipline, ROI defense, decision quality.

core_skills.name: Political Acumen
core_skills.description: Reading power maps; knowing when to push, when to wait.

core_skills.name: Coalition Building
core_skills.description: Aligning peers and functions across reporting lines.

core_skills.name: Stage-Gate Discipline
core_skills.description: Hitting milestones investors and sponsors track.

core_skills.name: ROI Defense
core_skills.description: Defending value vs internal alternatives in dollars.

core_skills.name: Vision Setting
core_skills.description: Articulating a 3-year picture that survives reorgs.

llm_config.audience_default: Senior Director leading an internal innovation project at a Fortune-500

hallmarks: Spends political capital on sponsor mapping (CDO co-sponsorship) before OKRs
Submits ambitious OKRs with calibration confidence — not safe ones
Pre-empts the immune system with a 4-page memo + cannibalization math
Takes an external paid pilot — real revenue beats internal funny-money
Launches standalone with a separate P&L when G6 thesis is validated
Poaches a senior PM from the core BU — guarantees an immune-system response
Submits 90% confidence OKRs — board reads it as low ambition
Escalates to the CEO at Q3 — burns political capital you'll need at G6
Submits a vague SWOT with a $4M ask — gets a 30% cut
Folds into the core BU without arguing for the standalone case

rounds.title: Q1 — Write the Charter
rounds.scenario: You have 60 days to deliver the project charter to the CEO. Three things compete for your time: securing a second C-level sponsor (Vikram, the CDO), pre-emptively bringing Atlas Legal into scoping conversations, and recruiting a senior PM from the core BU.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Senior director writing on a glass wall in a corporate war room, post-it notes, blueprints

choices.label: Spend a week with the CDO Vikram, get him formally co-sponsoring
choices.feedback: Smart. Two C-suite sponsors creates redundancy and political cover.

decision_record.rationale: C-suite redundancy is the highest-leverage move at G1

choices.expert_rationale: CDO co-sponsorship creates the redundancy that survives a CEO calendar shift. Sponsor mapping is the highest-leverage move at G1 — before code, before customers, before OKRs.

choices.label: Pre-empt Legal — invite GC to scope the data-privacy plan now
choices.feedback: Counterintuitive but right. Legal-as-blocker turns into legal-as-co-author.

decision_record.rationale: Legal early > Legal late — saves 6+ weeks at G3

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Inviting Legal to scope at G1 is well-intentioned but creates a process gate before you have a thesis. Legal's job is to slow things down — give them something to scope first.

choices.label: Poach a senior PM from the core BU — quietly
choices.feedback: You got the PM but the core BU P&L owner now treats you as a thief.

spend_political_capital.reason: Forced talent pull from core BU

decision_record.rationale: Talent matters but cost was the BU war

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Quietly poaching from the core BU guarantees the immune-system response in Q3. The cost of one PM is two quarters of political defense.

rounds.title: Q2 — Set Your OKRs
rounds.scenario: Vikram (CDO) wants to see your Q1-Q2 OKRs before approving the G2 budget unlock. He'll forward them to the steering committee. The OKRs you write here will be graded against senior-operator standards and used to track your stage-gate progression.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: OKR sticky notes on a glass wall, marker drawings of arrows and metrics

choices.label: Submit ambitious OKRs (3 obj × 3 KRs each, 60% confidence)
choices.feedback: Vikram likes the ambition. He warned you that the steering committee will hold you to them.
choices.expert_rationale: 3 obj × 3 KRs at 60% confidence is what serious intrapreneurs submit — boards read it as conviction. The calibration data lets you defend the variance later.

choices.label: Submit conservative OKRs (2 obj × 2 KRs, 90% confidence)
choices.feedback: Sandbagging. Vikram noticed and lost some faith — but the steerco won't kill you.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 90% confidence OKRs are read as low ambition. The board wants to see the upside — calibrate the risk, don't hide from it.

choices.label: Push OKR finalization a quarter — 'we need more discovery'
choices.feedback: Stage-gates don't reward delay. You burned political capital and Vikram is annoyed.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'Need more discovery' is the phrase that loses you the gate. The committee assumes you're stalling.

rounds.title: Q3 — The Immune System Awakens
rounds.scenario: The core BU P&L owner has been quietly building a case to your CFO that your skunkworks is duplicative of an existing roadmap item. You hear about it at lunch from a friendly VP. Your G3 alpha review is in 6 weeks.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Corporate boardroom power dynamics, two executives debating across a polished table

choices.label: Pre-empt with a 4-page memo: market gap analysis + cannibalization math
choices.feedback: Right play. You made the CFO neutral and the core BU P&L owner blink. Memo went to steerco.

decision_record.rationale: Data > narrative when CFO is the audience

choices.expert_rationale: A 4-page memo with market gap analysis + cannibalization math kills the immune-system attack at the analytical level. Marcus loses the political fight because the math is on the page.

choices.label: Escalate to the CEO — ask her to publicly back the project
choices.feedback: She backed you publicly but you spent C-suite political capital. Other VPs noticed.

sponsor_alignment.concern: CEO had to bail you out

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Escalating to the CEO at Q3 burns political capital you need at G6. The CEO doesn't want to be the referee.

choices.label: Ignore — focus on alpha; trust the work to speak
choices.feedback: It didn't speak. The memo went to the steerco anyway. You're now defending against a position you didn't see.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Ignoring an immune-system attack means it metastasizes. Marcus tells three more SVPs and now you have a coalition against you.

inbox_events.subject: I just heard about your pilot
inbox_events.body: Stop poaching my engineers and stay out of enterprise accounts. We talk Friday.

choices.label: Stand firm — clarify charter scope on Friday
Back off enterprise accounts for now

rounds.title: Q4 — SWOT for the SteerCo
rounds.scenario: G4 is the steering committee gate. The CDO wants you to walk in with a clean SWOT vs the two leading external incumbents and a clear capital-allocation ask for G5 pilot ($2.5M). The steerco includes the CFO who has signaled skepticism.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Steering committee in a glass-walled boardroom, slide on screen, executives leaning forward

choices.label: Submit a 4-cell SWOT + a phased $2.5M pilot ask with stop-loss criteria
choices.feedback: You hit the discipline notes the CFO needed. Pilot approved with conditions.
choices.expert_rationale: A 4-cell SWOT + phased $2.5M ask with stop-loss criteria is the steering-committee dream brief. You're handing them a calibrated bet, not a wish.

choices.label: Submit a generic SWOT + an aggressive $4M pilot ask
choices.feedback: The CFO killed the ask down to $1.5M. You over-asked and lost momentum.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Generic SWOT + $4M ask gets a 30% cut on principle. The committee can't approve what they can't audit.

choices.label: Skip SWOT — lead with a customer pilot story and a $2.5M ask
choices.feedback: Customer story landed but the CFO's data-needy questions weren't answered. Funded but on a leash.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Skipping SWOT and leading with a customer story is what people do when they don't have the data. The CFO notices.

rounds.title: Q5 — Pilot Customer Reality
rounds.scenario: You have two pilot candidates: (a) a friendly Atlas business unit that will pay you internally with funny money, or (b) a real external customer in a regulated vertical (healthcare) who will sign a paid contract — but legal wants 8 more weeks of review.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Two contracts side by side on a desk, executive deciding

choices.label: Take the external paid pilot — wait for legal
choices.feedback: Real revenue, real validation. But the 8-week delay forced a Q6 launch slip.

decision_record.rationale: External revenue is the only signal that matters at G5

forecast_prompt.question: Forecast pilot-to-paid conversion rate after the 90-day window. Provide an 80% CI as a percentage (e.g. 8 to 22).

choices.expert_rationale: External paid revenue is the only signal that survives the next steering review. The legal delay is real but the revenue is bankable. Internal pilots create transfer-pricing arguments.

choices.label: Run the internal Atlas BU pilot first — speed > validation
choices.feedback: Fast but the 'win' looked like an internal favor. Steerco discounted it 50%.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Speed without external validation is how skunkworks get killed at G5 — the question becomes 'why couldn't we just sell this to ourselves?'

rounds.title: Q6 — Launch or Land?
rounds.scenario: G6 is here. The CEO is asking whether to launch as a standalone Atlas brand or fold the product into the core BU's roadmap (the BU lead is now neutral after Q3).
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Corporate launch event with executives shaking hands, blue stage lights

choices.label: Launch as standalone Atlas brand — full commercial team, separate P&L
choices.feedback: High variance: 3-yr revenue ceiling much higher, but standalone needs core BU forbearance.
choices.expert_rationale: Standalone Atlas brand + separate P&L is what the G6 ask was always for. Folding back into the BU at G6 invalidates the political capital you spent at G3.

choices.label: Fold into core BU — accept as feature in the parent product
choices.feedback: Lower ceiling but immediate distribution. The BU lead becomes a friend.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Folding into the core BU at G6 is the immune-system winning quietly. Marcus celebrates; your team rotates out.

choices.label: Kill the project on your own terms; ship the learnings
choices.feedback: Hard call. You preserved political capital and Atlas didn't waste $4M chasing a Q5 signal that didn't pan out.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Killing on your terms is the right move when the market signal is negative — but at G6 with a paid pilot, it's a confidence loss.

score_bands.label: Founder-grade intrapreneur
score_bands.feedback: You navigated the immune system, defended ROI, and made the steering committee look smart. Atlas should give you a budget every year.

score_bands.label: Strong intrapreneurial run
score_bands.feedback: Solid stage-gate discipline. Tighten your political-capital math next time.

score_bands.label: Mixed — survived but bruised
score_bands.feedback: You launched but burned more sponsors and political capital than necessary.

score_bands.label: Killed by the immune system
score_bands.feedback: Re-run focusing on coalition building and pre-empting legal/CISO at G1, not G3.

glossary_terms.definition: A funding milestone where a steering committee reviews evidence and either releases more capital or kills the project.
Discretionary trust you can spend to push decisions through; replenished slowly via wins, depleted quickly by overreach.
How aligned a senior executive is with your project's goals; high alignment = they defend you in your absence.
Functions (legal, finance, IT, CISO, core BU) whose job is to protect the parent — they will resist new things by default.
Quantifying your project's value vs internal alternatives, in dollars the CFO recognizes.

coaching_moment.title: Politics is a feature, not a bug
coaching_moment.body: Skunkworks teams die from corporate antibodies, not technical failure. Your job isn't just to ship — it's to keep the host organisation invested enough that they don't reject you. Pick your sponsors and your enemies on purpose.

reflection_prompt: Which lever, if you'd moved it earlier, would have changed your outcome the most?
